parts.label: (a)(i)
hints: Hint 1: Think about what happens to the kinetic energy of a fast electron when it passes close to a positive nucleus in the target - does it keep all its speed or lose some?
Hint 2: Consider whether every electron loses exactly the same amount of energy in one hit, or if there are many possible amounts of energy loss.
Hint 3: Link the energy lost by an electron in a single interaction to the energy, and so frequency, of the single photon that is created.
parts.proper_answer: Incident electrons are decelerated by the target nuclei and lose kinetic energy as X-ray photons (bremsstrahlung). Different electrons undergo different amounts of deceleration, so different amounts of energy are lost. Photon energy equals energy lost, giving a continuous range of photon energies.
walkthrough:
Step 1: **What produces the X-rays - braking radiation**
Think of the fast electrons crashing into the metal. As an electron passes near a positively charged nucleus it is attracted and sharply slowed down, or decelerated. The kinetic energy it loses does not disappear, it is emitted as a single X-ray photon. This is called bremsstrahlung or braking radiation.

Step 2: **Why not all the same energy**
Not every electron has the same close encounter. Some pass very close and stop almost completely, some are only slightly deflected, and many suffer multiple smaller collisions. So there is a whole range of possible decelerations and a whole range of possible energy losses.

Step 3: **From energy loss to continuous spectrum**
For one interaction: $$E_{photon} = \text{energy lost by electron}$$ A large deceleration gives a high-energy photon, a small deceleration gives a low-energy photon. Because the deceleration can take any value up to a maximum, the photon energy takes any value up to a maximum, which is a continuous spectrum.

parts.label: (a)(ii)
hints: Hint 1: Start by thinking when the photon energy is largest - what must happen to the full 15 keV of kinetic energy gained by an electron?
Hint 2: Recall how to connect electron kinetic energy from the accelerating voltage to photon energy from its wavelength using $eV$ and $hc/\lambda$.
parts.proper_answer: Maximum photon energy = $eV = hc/\lambda_{min}$. $\lambda_{min} = hc/(eV) = 8.3 \times 10^{-11} \text{ m}$.
walkthrough:
Step 1: **Highest energy means full energy in one photon**
An electron accelerated through $V = 15 \text{ kV}$ gains kinetic energy: $$E_{max} = eV$$ The most energetic X-ray is made when one electron gives all of this energy to a single photon in one violent stop. So: $$E_{photon,max} = eV = \frac{hc}{\lambda_{min}}$$

Step 2: **Rearrange for minimum wavelength**
Highest energy means smallest wavelength, since $E = hc/\lambda$. Rearranging: $$\lambda_{min} = \frac{hc}{eV}$$

Step 3: **Put in numbers**
$$V = 15000 \text{ V}$$ $$\lambda_{min} = \frac{(6.63 \times 10^{-34})(3.0 \times 10^{8})}{(1.60 \times 10^{-19})(15000)}$$ $$\lambda_{min} = \frac{1.989 \times 10^{-25}}{2.40 \times 10^{-15}} \approx 8.3 \times 10^{-11} \text{ m}$$ This is the short-wavelength limit of the continuous spectrum.

parts.label: (b)(i)
hints: Hint 1: Recall the linearised form of the attenuation law - what does a graph of $\ln(I/I_{o})$ against $x$ look like and what is its gradient in terms of $\mu$?
Hint 2: Pick two widely spaced, easy-to-read points on the straight line in Fig. 11.1 to find rise over run and so $\mu$ with unit $\text{cm}^{-1}$.
parts.proper_answer: $\ln(I/I_{o}) = -\mu x$, so $\mu = -$ gradient. Gradient $\approx -0.21$, giving $\mu \approx 0.21 \text{ cm}^{-1}$.
walkthrough:
Step 1: **Linearise the exponential**
Intensity falls exponentially: $$I = I_{o}e^{-\mu x}$$ Taking natural logs: $$\ln\left(\frac{I}{I_{o}}\right) = -\mu x$$ So a plot of $\ln(I/I_{o})$ against $x$ is a straight line through the origin with gradient $= -\mu$.

Step 2: **Find the gradient from Fig. 11.1**
Read off the line. For example at $x = 10.0 \text{ cm}$, $\ln(I/I_{o}) \approx -2.08$. Then: $$\mu = -\frac{\Delta \ln(I/I_{o})}{\Delta x} = -\frac{-2.08 - 0}{10.0 - 0}$$ $$\mu \approx 0.21 \text{ cm}^{-1}$$ Any large triangle gives $0.20$ to $0.22 \text{ cm}^{-1}$.

parts.label: (b)(ii)
hints: Hint 1: Translate 5.0% of initial intensity into a value for the ratio $I/I_{o}$ and then for $\ln(I/I_{o})$.
Hint 2: Use your value of $\mu$ from (b)(i) in $\ln(I/I_{o}) = -\mu x$ and solve for the thickness $x$.
walkthrough:
Step 1: **Set up the required fraction**
Reduced to 5.0% means: $$\frac{I}{I_{o}} = 0.050$$ Insert into the attenuation law: $$\ln(0.050) = -\mu x$$ where $\ln(0.050) \approx -3.00$.

Step 2: **Solve for thickness**
Using $\mu \approx 0.21 \text{ cm}^{-1}$: $$x = \frac{-\ln(0.050)}{\mu} = \frac{3.00}{0.21}$$ $$x \approx 14 \text{ cm}$$ A thicker layer is needed because tissue is not very absorbing for this beam.
